summary: Considers what a host should do when a message sent over the early network does not get a normal reply. The IMP can return different message types depending on whether the destination IMP or its host interface is down. It suggests how to handle those cases and time-outs.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 142 proposes a time limit for waiting on connection and close commands so NCP resources do not stay occupied indefinitely. It also identifies an unresolved race if a late close arrives after a new request uses the same sockets.

questions: how should a host handle time-outs in the host-host protocol
what happens when a destination imp is down
how do you recover from lost connections
why do network connections get stuck
subtitle: A proposed timeout for resolving unanswered Host-Host connection commands.

tldr.problem: After a connection or close command, the NCP can wait indefinitely for a matching response while sockets, links and table space remain occupied.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal uses a network-standard time limit T; after an unanswered STR or RTS it sends CLS, and after an unanswered CLS it assumes the matching CLS has returned.
tldr.outcome: The authors identify a race when a new connection uses the same socket pair before a late CLS arrives, and leave the value of T and the race for discussion.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 142 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC proposes a timeout mechanism but leaves the timeout value and a late-CLS race unresolved.

sections.title: When Commands Receive No Match
sections.content:
After sending to a foreign site, an IMP may return Type 7 or Type 9 messages for some failure conditions, or Type 5 (RFNM) when the destination interface is taking messages. The note focuses on what the Host-Host protocol should do if an NCP sends STR or RTS and then receives an RFNM but no matching RTS, STR or CLS arrives after a long time.

A similar problem occurs when a sent CLS never receives a matching CLS. Sockets, links and NCP table space remain tied up while the host waits.
sections.plainLanguage: A host can receive an RFNM but still wait a long time for the matching connection command. Waiting also holds sockets and other resources that the host might want to reuse.

sections.title: Timeout Actions for STR, RTS and CLS
sections.content:
If a sent STR or RTS has no matching RTS, STR or CLS within T time units, the proposal sends a CLS. It says the host can avoid one race by ignoring a matching RTS or STR that arrives before the matching CLS.

If a sent CLS receives no matching CLS within T time units, the host assumes the matching CLS has returned and frees the resources.
sections.plainLanguage: After waiting T time units for a connection response, the host sends CLS. If a close receives no matching close within T, the host treats it as completed and frees the resources.

sections.title: A Late Close Can Be Ambiguous
sections.content:
After timing out a CLS, a host may free the socket pair and send a new RTS or STR on it. If a CLS then arrives, the host cannot tell whether it matches the earlier close or refuses the new connection.

The authors say they have not solved this race and do not favor assigning network-wide sequence numbers to connections. They ask the Host-Host Protocol Glitch Cleaning Committee to consider the issue; the value of T also remains to be decided as a network standard.
sections.plainLanguage: A late CLS could refer to an old close or a new connection request on the same sockets. The note identifies this ambiguity but does not solve it.
